hints: Start from butane, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, and think where a single Br atom can replace a H atom to give a different carbon skeleton connectivity.
Number the longest carbon chain to give Br the lowest number, then name as bromo + butane for each unique position.
walkthrough:
Picture what substitution does**
You start with straight chain butane. Ultraviolet light lets bromine replace one hydrogen with one bromine, so the formula becomes $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Br}$. The carbon chain stays four carbons long, only the position of Br can change.

Find the two different positions**
If Br goes on an end carbon you get $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$. If Br goes on an inner carbon you get $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(Br)CH}_{3}$. Putting Br on the other end or the other inner carbon just gives the same two structures flipped over, so there are only two.

Name them systematically**
Count to give Br the lowest number. Br on carbon 1 gives 1-bromobutane. Br on carbon 2 gives 2-bromobutane. Draw each as displayed or skeletal structures and write the matching name underneath.

Final answer: Isomer 1: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$, 1-bromobutane
Isomer 2: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(Br)CH}_{3}$, 2-bromobutane

hints: Compare the two structures from (a)(i): the carbon skeleton and functional group are the same, only the location of Br on the chain differs.
walkthrough:
Link the difference to the definition**
Both molecules have the same skeleton, butane, and the same functional group, Br. The only difference is where Br is attached, carbon 1 compared with carbon 2. When the position of a substituent differs in this way, we call it positional isomerism.

hints: Look for a carbon with four single bonds to four completely different atoms or groups in Fig. 4.1.
walkthrough:
Test each carbon for four different groups**
A chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups. The left carbon in halothane is $\text{CF}_{3}$, it has three identical F atoms, so it cannot be chiral. The right carbon is bonded to H, to Br, to Cl and to $\text{CF}_{3}$. All four are different, so it is tetrahedral and chiral.

Mark it clearly**
Place an asterisk * next to that right-hand carbon, the $\text{C}^{*}(\text{H})(\text{Br})(\text{Cl})(\text{CF}_{3})$ carbon.
Final answer: Chiral centre is the right-hand C in Fig. 4.1, the $\text{CHBrCl}$ carbon bonded to H, Br, Cl and $\text{CF}_{3}$, marked with *.

hints: Recall that homolytic fission splits a covalent bond so each atom keeps one electron from the shared pair, forming two radicals shown with a dot.
walkthrough:
Split the C-Br bond evenly**
Homolytic means equal. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond pair does not both go to one atom. One electron stays on carbon and one goes to bromine. That gives two neutral radicals, each with an unpaired electron.

Write the radical equation**
Halothane $\text{CF}_{3}\text{CHBrCl}$ therefore gives a carbon centred radical $\text{CF}_{3}\text{\.{C}HCl}$ plus a bromine radical $\text{Br}^{\bullet}$. Show the dot for the unpaired electron on each product.
Final answer: $\text{CF}_{3}\text{CHBrCl} \rightarrow \text{CF}_{3}\text{\.{C}HCl} + \text{Br}^{\bullet}$

hints: Bromine is atomic number 35, so after [Ar] you need 17 more electrons to place in 3d, 4s and 4p, filling 4s before 3d and 4p last with Hund's rule.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons to place**
Br has 35 electrons. [Ar] accounts for 18, leaving 17. The order after Ar is 4s, then 3d, then 4p, giving $\text{4s}^{2}\text{3d}^{10}\text{4p}^{5}$.

Fill the boxes correctly**
The 3d set has five orbitals, so draw five boxes each with paired arrows $\uparrow\downarrow$. The 4s is one box with $\uparrow\downarrow$. The 4p set has three orbitals for five electrons, so fill $\uparrow\downarrow$ in the first, $\uparrow\downarrow$ in the second and a single $\uparrow$ in the third, with all single electrons having the same spin.

Final answer: [Ar] 3d: five boxes each $\uparrow\downarrow$ (10 electrons), 4s: one box $\uparrow\downarrow$ (2 electrons), 4p: three boxes $\uparrow\downarrow$, $\uparrow\downarrow$, $\uparrow$ (5 electrons).

hints: Identify the repeat unit in Fig. 4.3 as $-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl})-$ and remember addition polymerisation converts a C=C double bond into single bonds.
walkthrough:
Read the repeat unit**
Fig. 4.3 shows a two carbon backbone with a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ side chain, so the repeating section is $-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl})-$.

Reverse polymerisation**
To get the monomer, join the two backbone carbons with a double bond and remove the continuation bonds. That gives $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, 3-chloroprop-1-ene (allyl chloride)

hints: Think about the strong C-C and C-Cl bonds in an addition polymer and what happens if it is put in landfill or burned.
walkthrough:
Connect structure to disposal**
X is an addition polymer with a saturated carbon chain and polar but strong C-Cl bonds. Microorganisms cannot break it down, so it stays in landfill for many years and wastes land.

Consider burning as an alternative**
If you try to burn it, the chlorine forms acidic, toxic $\text{HCl}$ gas (and possibly dioxins), which causes air pollution and corrosion, so special treatment is needed. Either route makes disposal difficult.
Final answer: X is non-biodegradable and persists in landfill, or combustion produces toxic gases such as $\text{HCl}$.
